claims.text: High configurational entropy combined with modest atomic-size mismatch governs retention of a single-phase solid solution in equiatomic high-entropy nanoparticles.
A solid solution remains structurally and chemically stable when entropy of mixing sufficiently overcomes enthalpic driving forces for segregation.
If enthalpic driving forces are not overcome, phase separation or intermetallic-compound formation will occur.
The proposed initial material is a homogeneous, minimally segregated solid-solution nanoparticle containing five or more metals in near-equal atomic ratios.
The proposed initial nanoparticles have an average particle size of approximately 5–10 nm.
Annealing across 473–1923 K can trigger chemical ordering, segregation, or phase changes in the nanoparticles.
Atomic-radius differences and bonding preferences provide enthalpic driving forces for local phase separation.
At high temperature, entropy of mixing lowers the free energy of the equiatomic solid solution.
Entropy-driven lowering of free energy suppresses the enthalpic tendency of constituent elements to segregate.
Sufficiently strong atomic-size or electronic differences can overcome entropy-driven stabilization and lead to phase separation or intermetallic formation.
Competition between entropy-driven stabilization and enthalpy-driven ordering determines long-term nanoparticle stability under operating conditions.
Nanoparticles with sufficiently high configurational entropy will retain a homogeneous, single-phase structure and chemical uniformity at both 473 K and 1923 K.
Nanoparticles with larger effective atomic mismatch or lower effective mixing will exhibit segregation or secondary phases after extended high-temperature exposure.
The prediction is limited to exposures that permit atomic redistribution without extensive sintering or coarsening.
Reactive species in the operating environment may alter diffusion kinetics and invalidate the prediction.
Nanoparticle surface effects may cause deviations from bulk thermodynamic predictions.
